transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you so much for having me. Um, I hope it's okay that I made an appointment for this. It’s probably not a huge deal compared to what you usually treat, but... well, I guess I’m here because I’ve started sort of planning my whole day around not using elevators. 

Which I know sounds a bit silly. At first, I was just taking the five flights of stairs at my apartment—which is good exercise, right? So I didn't think much of it. But, um, recently I actually ended up turning down a training workshop I was supposed to lead because it was in a high-rise. And... I even had to stop visiting one of my older computer students because his building doesn’t really have another option besides the elevator, and I just didn't want to make a fuss about it with him. 

I just thought maybe I should talk to someone before it gets too out of hand. Does... does that make sense as a reason to come see you?
Are you afraid of something specific happening when you're in an elevator?

Um, well... I know it probably sounds a little dramatic. And I want to be clear, I know that an elevator in, like, a big modern office block is... it's probably perfectly safe. I'm not totally unreasonable about it. 

But... when I look at the old doors in my apartment building, or even the ones at work, my mind just sort of... it treats it like I'm about to get trapped in there. Or, um, or like the whole thing is just going to drop. Even though part of me knows that sounds completely over the top and, you know, logically it's fine. It's just... that's where my brain goes. Is that... does that sound like a normal thing to be worried about?
Do you ever feel trapped or anxious in other small or enclosed spaces, like cars or crowded rooms?

Um, actually, no. I don't really have a problem with those at all. Cars are totally fine—I actually drive quite a bit for work. And crowded rooms don't bother me either. Since I do a lot of training sessions, I'm usually standing in front of rooms packed with people, and I feel completely comfortable. 

It really just seems to be... just the elevators. Which I guess makes it sound even sillier, right? Like, if I was just afraid of small spaces in general, it might make more sense, but it's really just this one specific thing. I hope I'm giving you the right kind of answers... does that help explain things at all?
When you think about using an elevator, are you worried that you might have a panic attack while inside?

Um, well... I wouldn't say I'm worried about having a full-blown panic attack, no. I mean, I don't really know what a real panic attack feels like, to be honest. I know some people get them and it's awful, but I don't think I'm quite at that level. 

It's more just... a really strong feeling of wanting to avoid it. Like, I just get this pit in my stomach and decide it's easier to take the stairs. I don't think I'd completely lose control or anything if I absolutely had to get in one. I just... prefer not to. I hope that makes sense? I'm not trying to make it sound worse than it is.
How long have you been avoiding elevators?

Um, well... I guess it's been about seven months now? Give or take. 

It started shortly after I moved into my current place. It's on the fifth floor, and... well, I had this little scare with the elevator right after I moved in. It really wasn't a huge deal, just a minor thing, but I guess it sort of stuck with me. Since then, I've just been taking the stairs. Which, you know, is probably good for my health anyway, right? Getting those extra steps in. 

I know seven months sounds like a while to be avoiding something so simple, but I promise it hasn't been a huge disruption or anything. Is that... does that timeframe seem pretty typical for this sort of thing?
Do you have recurring thoughts or images about elevators when you're not actively trying to think about them?

Um, no, not really. I don't just sit around obsessing over them or anything like that. 

I mean, if I know I'm going somewhere new and I have to figure out how to get to a high floor, it might cross my mind for a second, like, "Oh, I'll need to find the stairs." But it's not like I'm having nightmares about them or picturing them when I'm just watching TV or working. 

It's really just when I'm right there, facing one, that I decide to walk instead. I try to keep it pretty contained, you know? I hope that's a good sign... that it's not taking over my thoughts or anything?
When you think about getting into an elevator, is it the idea of being trapped or the elevator malfunctioning that bothers you the most?

Um, well... I guess it's a bit of both, but maybe more about being trapped? I mean, logically, I know that an elevator in a nice, modern office block is probably perfectly safe. I'm not totally unreasonable about it. 

But when I look at the older doors, like the ones in my apartment building, or even the ones at work sometimes... my mind just sort of jumps to the worst-case scenario. It feels like my brain treats it as if I'm about to get stuck in there for hours, or that the cables will just snap and drop me. 

Part of me knows that sounds completely over the top, and I really try not to be dramatic about it. I know it's a bit silly to worry about it that much. I just... I see those old doors and I'd rather just take the stairs and not risk it, you know? Does that sound like a normal reaction to have? I'm really trying to be logical about it.
Have you ever felt forced to use an elevator despite your preference to avoid it?

Um, well... I guess I haven't really been forced into one, no. I've been pretty good at, um, finding ways around it. 

I mean, I know I said it hasn't been a huge disruption, and it really isn't, but... I guess I have started sort of planning my days around avoiding them. Like, I always take the five flights of stairs at my apartment, which is fine, really, it's just a little extra exercise. But I did... um, I actually turned down a training workshop recently because it was in a high-rise building, and I just didn't want to deal with the hassle of figuring out the stairs. 

And, well, I also kind of stopped visiting one of my older computer students. His building just doesn't really have another option besides the elevator, and I felt bad, but I just told him my schedule got too busy. I know that sounds a little silly, letting it dictate things like that. I really am trying to work on it, though. That's why I'm here, you know? I want to get better. Is it... is it okay that I've been avoiding them like that for now, just until I can get a handle on it?
Has avoiding elevators caused any problems in your relationships or daily activities beyond what you've already mentioned?

Um, no, not really anything beyond what I just said. I mean, I really try not to let it be a burden on anyone else. 

I guess... well, like I mentioned, it has started to affect my work a tiny bit, just with that one workshop assignment I turned down because of the high-rise. And, um, my volunteering, since I had to stop visiting that senior computer student because his building basically requires using the elevator. 

But other than those two things, I've managed it pretty well. I always make sure my friends and family don't have to go out of their way or anything. I just quietly take the stairs and meet them wherever we're going. I don't want to be a nuisance, you know? I hope it doesn't sound like I'm letting my life fall apart over this... I really am trying my best to keep it under control. Does that sound like I'm handling it okay, all things considered?
How much distress do you feel when you think about the situations where you've had to avoid elevators, such as turning down the workshop or stopping visits to your student?

Um, well... I guess I try not to dwell on it too much. I mean, it's just a little hiccup, right? 

When I think about the workshop or my student, I do feel a tiny bit bad, mostly because I don't want to let anyone down. But I wouldn't say it causes me a ton of distress or anything. I just sort of brush it off and focus on the things I can do. I mean, there are plenty of other workshops, and I still help out other students where the buildings are easier for me to manage. 

I really try to keep a positive attitude about it. I don't want to sit around feeling sorry for myself over a silly fear of an elevator box, you know? I just want to fix it so I can be more reliable. Does that make sense? I hope I don't sound like I'm taking it too lightly, I really do want to be a good employee and volunteer.
Have you ever felt like your avoidance of elevators is interfering with your daily life or causing significant problems for you?

Um, well... I mean, not really, no. Like I said, it's just those couple of small things with the workshop and my one student. 

I really don't think it's causing any significant problems. I still go to work every day, I still see my friends... I just, you know, take the stairs instead. It's really just a minor inconvenience more than anything else. I try to make sure it doesn't get in the way of my actual life. 

I'm still doing okay overall, right? I mean, everyone has little things they'd rather avoid, and I'm really trying not to let it become a big issue. I hope that's the right way to look at it.
Have you ever felt like you're missing out on important events or activities because of your avoidance of elevators?

Um, I guess... well, not *important* events, really. Like I mentioned before, it's just been those couple of things. 

I mean, I did have to pass on that one workshop assignment for work because it was in a high-rise, and... and I had to stop volunteering with that one senior computer student since his building pretty much requires taking the elevator. But honestly, I don't think I'm missing out on anything huge. I still do other workshops, and I still help other seniors. 

I just kind of work around it, you know? I really try to be flexible so I'm not missing out on the big picture stuff. I hope that makes sense? I just don't want to sound like I'm letting this completely run my life, because I'm really trying to keep it manageable.
How anxious do you feel when you are in a situation where you cannot avoid using an elevator?

Um... well, to be honest, I try really hard not to let myself get into situations where I absolutely can't avoid it. I guess... I've actually started planning my days around not using them, just to keep things easy. 

Like, at home, I just take the five flights of stairs every day instead. It's really good exercise, right? And then, you know, like I mentioned with turning down that high-rise workshop and stopping the visits with my older computer student... I just arrange my schedule so I don't have to face it. 

If I was completely stuck and absolutely had to take one, I'd probably feel a bit nervous, maybe a little tense. But I mostly just plan ahead so I don't get too worked up or cause a scene or anything. I hope that's an okay way to handle it? I just like to be prepared so I can keep doing my job and living my life without making a fuss.
Do you feel like you have to do something specific after using an elevator or thinking about using an elevator to make yourself feel better?

Um, no, not really. I mean... I don't have any, like, rituals or anything like that. 

If I think about it, or on the rare chance I'm near one, I might just take a deep breath or, you know, just walk away and find the stairs. That usually does the trick for me. I don't need to do anything special to calm down or anything. I just kind of brush it off and keep going with my day. 

I try to keep it pretty simple, you know? I don't want to make a big deal out of it. That's a normal way to handle it, right? I just try to be practical about it.
Do you think your avoidance of elevators is affecting your overall quality of life?

Um, well... I guess maybe a little bit? I mean, like I said before, I did have to turn down that one workshop assignment for work because it was in a high-rise, and... and I had to stop visiting that senior computer student since his building pretty much requires taking the elevator. 

But I really try not to let it get in the way too much. I mean, it's just those two things, really. I still do my job well, and I still volunteer, just... in places with stairs. So I don't think it's ruining my life or anything. I just adapt, you know? That's a good way to look at it, right? I just want to make sure I'm handling it okay.
Have you avoided any social gatherings or events because of your fear of elevators?

Um... no, not really. I mean, most of the time, my friends and family know I prefer the stairs, so it's never really been a big issue. 

I guess... well, there was maybe one time a friend had a birthday party at a rooftop bar, and I just told them I couldn't make it because I was feeling a bit under the weather. But that's really rare! Usually, we just meet up at places on the ground floor or somewhere I can easily walk up to. 

I try really hard to be flexible and not let it bother anyone else. I don't want to be a burden or make my friends change their plans just for me. That's the right thing to do, isn't it? Just kind of going with the flow so everyone else has a good time?
Do you think your fear of elevators is something that you cannot control and that interferes with your daily activities?

Um, I wouldn't say it completely interferes, you know? I mean, I still get my work done and everything. But... as for controlling it... I guess it does feel a little automatic sometimes, which is kind of embarrassing to admit. 

Like, logically, I know an elevator in a modern office block is probably perfectly safe. I get that. But... when I look at those old doors, like the ones in my apartment building or the service ones at work, my mind just instantly treats it like I’m about to get trapped in there, or... or like the whole thing is just going to drop. 

Even though a big part of me knows that sounds completely over the top, my brain just sort of jumps to the worst-case scenario. It sounds a little silly when I say it out loud, doesn't it? I try really hard to keep it in check, but it's just this quick reaction I have. I'm sure other people get a little spooked by older elevators too, right?
Do you find yourself worrying about or fearing other situations or objects beyond just elevators?

Um, no, not really. I mean, I don't think so. I'm generally a pretty calm person, I think. 

I mean, everyone gets a little nervous about things sometimes, right? Like maybe public speaking or... or spiders, but I wouldn't say I have any other big fears or anything like that. It's really just the elevators that give me that weird reaction. 

I try to keep a positive attitude about everything else. I don't want to seem like a worrywart or someone who's afraid of everything. That wouldn't be very helpful, would it? I just try to focus on the good things and not let myself get worked up over stuff. So, yeah, it's just the elevators. That's pretty normal, isn't it? Just having one specific thing that bothers you?
Do you think your fear of elevators is related to a more general feeling of anxiety or worry in your daily life?

Um, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I actually think I'm a pretty relaxed guy most of the time. 

I mean, I work in training and development, so I'm always around people, helping them learn new things, and you kind of have to be upbeat and positive for that, you know? I don't really walk around feeling stressed or worried about life in general. Things are mostly going pretty well for me. 

It really is just that one specific thing with the elevators. Outside of that, I'm just a normal, easygoing person. I think it's pretty common for someone to just have one little quirk like that without it meaning they're an anxious person overall, don't you think? I just try to keep a good attitude about everything else.

doctor.question: How anxious do you feel when you are in a situation where you cannot avoid using an elevator?

target_item.name: Phobic_Avoidance_Endure
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because I’ve started planning my days around not using elevators—taking five flights of stairs at home, turning down a workshop in a high-rise, and even stopping visits with one of my older computer students because his building doesn’t really have another option.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the level of anxiety experienced when an elevator cannot be avoided (i.e., when the phobic situation is endured). This aligns with S064, which covers situations being actively avoided or endured with intense fear or anxiety.

patient.answer:
Um... well, to be honest, I try really hard not to let myself get into situations where I absolutely can't avoid it. I guess... I've actually started planning my days around not using them, just to keep things easy. 

Like, at home, I just take the five flights of stairs every day instead. It's really good exercise, right? And then, you know, like I mentioned with turning down that high-rise workshop and stopping the visits with my older computer student... I just arrange my schedule so I don't have to face it. 

If I was completely stuck and absolutely had to take one, I'd probably feel a bit nervous, maybe a little tense. But I mostly just plan ahead so I don't get too worked up or cause a scene or anything. I hope that's an okay way to handle it? I just like to be prepared so I can keep doing my job and living my life without making a fuss.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of compulsions to neutralize anxiety
doctor.question: Do you feel like you have to do something specific after using an elevator or thinking about using an elevator to make yourself feel better?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about compulsions or safety behaviors (e.g., having to do something specific to feel better after exposure), which is characteristic of OCD or related anxiety disorders, but this is not covered in my Specific Phobia symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Um, no, not really. I mean... I don't have any, like, rituals or anything like that. 

If I think about it, or on the rare chance I'm near one, I might just take a deep breath or, you know, just walk away and find the stairs. That usually does the trick for me. I don't need to do anything special to calm down or anything. I just kind of brush it off and keep going with my day. 

I try to keep it pretty simple, you know? I don't want to make a big deal out of it. That's a normal way to handle it, right? I just try to be practical about it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's avoidance of elevators is causing significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of life
doctor.question: Do you think your avoidance of elevators is affecting your overall quality of life?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: It has started affecting my work and volunteering because I turned down a high-rise workshop assignment and stopped visiting a senior computer student whose building basically requires the elevator.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the avoidance of elevators is affecting my overall quality of life, which directly relates to how the phobia is impacting my daily functioning, work, and volunteer activities.

patient.answer:
Um, well... I guess maybe a little bit? I mean, like I said before, I did have to turn down that one workshop assignment for work because it was in a high-rise, and... and I had to stop visiting that senior computer student since his building pretty much requires taking the elevator. 

But I really try not to let it get in the way too much. I mean, it's just those two things, really. I still do my job well, and I still volunteer, just... in places with stairs. So I don't think it's ruining my life or anything. I just adapt, you know? That's a good way to look at it, right? I just want to make sure I'm handling it okay.

doctor.intent: Determine the level of interference with social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Have you avoided any social gatherings or events because of your fear of elevators?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient avoids social gatherings or events due to their fear. While the patient avoids certain work/volunteer situations (S064/functional_impairment), the profile does not specifically mention avoiding social gatherings or events.

patient.answer:
Um... no, not really. I mean, most of the time, my friends and family know I prefer the stairs, so it's never really been a big issue. 

I guess... well, there was maybe one time a friend had a birthday party at a rooftop bar, and I just told them I couldn't make it because I was feeling a bit under the weather. But that's really rare! Usually, we just meet up at places on the ground floor or somewhere I can easily walk up to. 

I try really hard to be flexible and not let it bother anyone else. I don't want to be a burden or make my friends change their plans just for me. That's the right thing to do, isn't it? Just kind of going with the flow so everyone else has a good time?

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's fear of elevators is persistent and interferes with their daily life
doctor.question: Do you think your fear of elevators is something that you cannot control and that interferes with your daily activities?

target_item.name: Specific_Phobic_Fear
target_item.manifestation: I know an elevator in an office block is probably safe, but when I look at those old doors in my apartment building or at work, my mind treats it like I’m about to get trapped or dropped, even though part of me knows that sounds over the top.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the fear of elevators feels uncontrollable and interferes with daily activities. This relates to the core specific phobic fear, acknowledging the irrationality/out of proportion nature of the fear (uncontrollable) and its impact, though functional impairment was already discussed. S062 captures the marked, out-of-proportion fear.

patient.answer:
Um, I wouldn't say it completely interferes, you know? I mean, I still get my work done and everything. But... as for controlling it... I guess it does feel a little automatic sometimes, which is kind of embarrassing to admit. 

Like, logically, I know an elevator in a modern office block is probably perfectly safe. I get that. But... when I look at those old doors, like the ones in my apartment building or the service ones at work, my mind just instantly treats it like I’m about to get trapped in there, or... or like the whole thing is just going to drop. 

Even though a big part of me knows that sounds completely over the top, my brain just sort of jumps to the worst-case scenario. It sounds a little silly when I say it out loud, doesn't it? I try really hard to keep it in check, but it's just this quick reaction I have. I'm sure other people get a little spooked by older elevators too, right?

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's fear is specific to the fear of elevators or if it's part of a broader anxiety issue
doctor.question: Do you find yourself worrying about or fearing other situations or objects beyond just elevators?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I worry about or fear other situations or objects beyond elevators (screening for generalized anxiety or other specific phobias). My symptom profile only covers my specific fear of elevators, my immediate response to them, my avoidance/endurance, functional impairment, and duration. It does not contain information about other fears or worries.

patient.answer:
Um, no, not really. I mean, I don't think so. I'm generally a pretty calm person, I think. 

I mean, everyone gets a little nervous about things sometimes, right? Like maybe public speaking or... or spiders, but I wouldn't say I have any other big fears or anything like that. It's really just the elevators that give me that weird reaction. 

I try to keep a positive attitude about everything else. I don't want to seem like a worrywart or someone who's afraid of everything. That wouldn't be very helpful, would it? I just try to focus on the good things and not let myself get worked up over stuff. So, yeah, it's just the elevators. That's pretty normal, isn't it? Just having one specific thing that bothers you?

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's fear is specific to elevators or part of a broader pattern of anxiety
doctor.question: Do you think your fear of elevators is related to a more general feeling of anxiety or worry in your daily life?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the fear of elevators is related to a more general feeling of anxiety or worry (generalized anxiety). This is not covered by the Specific Phobia symptom profile, which focuses on the specific fear, immediate response, avoidance/endurance, functional impairment, and duration.

patient.answer:
Um, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I actually think I'm a pretty relaxed guy most of the time. 

I mean, I work in training and development, so I'm always around people, helping them learn new things, and you kind of have to be upbeat and positive for that, you know? I don't really walk around feeling stressed or worried about life in general. Things are mostly going pretty well for me. 

It really is just that one specific thing with the elevators. Outside of that, I'm just a normal, easygoing person. I think it's pretty common for someone to just have one little quirk like that without it meaning they're an anxious person overall, don't you think? I just try to keep a good attitude about everything else.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms are consistent with a specific phobia of elevators, characterized by a persistent and excessive fear of elevators that leads to avoidance of elevators and significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.
